|---:|---:|---|---|---|
| India | 99.6% (₹15,634.80 mn of ₹15,690.42 mn consolidated revenue from external customers, FY26) | Stable — 99.6% FY26, 99.6% FY25 (₹13,830.01 mn of ₹13,883.44 mn), 99.5% FY24 (₹11,903.62 mn of ₹11,967.75 mn) | FY26 Annual Report (Ind AS), Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements, "Information about geographical areas" (revenue from external customers by location of operations, Web-and-related-services + Accounting Software services combined) | High — the business is, for practical purposes, a single-country revenue stream |
| Other than India | 0.4% (₹55.62 mn of ₹15,690.42 mn, FY26) | Stable / marginal — ₹53.43 mn FY25, ₹64.13 mn FY24; no sustained growth trend visible across three years | Same FY26 Annual Report note as above | Low in isolation (too small to matter), but the flat trend shows international/export revenue (linked to the Platinum-tier "international RFQs" feature) has not scaled | 

Non-current assets by location mirror the revenue split: ₹4,968.03 mn in India versus ₹0 outside India as at 31 March 2026 (FY26 Annual Report, same note) — the company has no disclosed physical footprint outside India either.

## 3. Concentration Flags

| Concentration Flag | Triggered (Y/N) | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| One customer >20% of revenue | N | FY26 Annual Report segment note: "No single customer represents 10% or more of the Group's total revenue for the year ended 31 March 2026 and 31 March 2025." No single-name customer disclosure exists to test above 10%, but the filing's own 10% test is negative. |
| Top 3 customers >40% of revenue | Not disclosed at the named-3-customer level (no such breakout exists). A related but not identical metric is disclosed and is well above 40%: the top 10% of paying suppliers (roughly 22,000 accounts, not 3) contributed 49% of FY26 revenue [FY26 Integrated Annual Report, p.83]. Treat the literal top-3 test as "Not disclosed," and flag the top-decile figure separately — the units are not the same. |
| One geography >50% of revenue | Y | India = 99.6% of FY26 consolidated revenue from external customers [FY26 Annual Report, "Information about geographical areas"]. |
| One customer or geography >30% with no long-term contract disclosed | Y | India geography (99.6% of revenue, no long-term contracts — revenue is subscription-based and collected in advance) and the Gold+Platinum paying-supplier cohort (~75% of revenue, renewed annually/monthly with no multi-year lock-in disclosed) both clear 30% with no long-term contract evidence. Credit-risk note confirms the model: "The Group majorly collects consideration in advance for the services to be provided to the customer" [FY26 Annual Report (Ind AS), Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements, Financial Risk Management — Credit risk]. |

## 4. Read

This is a geography-concentrated business layered on top of a customer base that is widening its dependence on a shrinking top slice of accounts. On geography, it is close to a single-country business: 99.6% of FY26 revenue and 100% of non-current assets sit in India, despite the company's own risk-management section claiming "diversified market presence across industries and geographies for risk distribution" [FY26 Annual Report, Risk Management, Economic Risk mitigation] — a claim the company's own segment note does not support. On the customer side, no single named account exceeds 10% of revenue, but the top 10% of paying suppliers already generate 49% of revenue and that share has risen every year since FY21 (41% → 49%), while the Gold-and-Platinum tier (about half the paying-supplier base) contributes nearly 75% of revenue. All of this is naked, not contractually secured — subscriptions are annual/monthly with no disclosed multi-year lock-in, and cash is simply collected in advance. The single biggest dependency for the synthesizer: IndiaMART's revenue is almost entirely a bet on Indian SME subscription spending (99.6% of revenue, one country, one buyer segment — small and mid-sized Indian sellers), with no geographic offset if that spending slows, and an increasing share of that revenue is concentrated in the willingness of the top-decile of paying suppliers to keep upgrading and renewing.

## business-model / 06_value-chain.md

_Source: `business-model/06_value-chain.md`_

# Value Chain Position — INDIAMART

## 1. Stages Occupied

IndiaMART is a two-sided digital marketplace, not a physical-goods business — the standard raw-material/manufacturer/distributor ladder does not apply. Its "value chain" is really: (a) what it buys to run the platform (labor, outsourced telesales, cloud/hosting, third-party data verification), and (b) the two sides of its marketplace — paying suppliers (who pay to be found) and buyers (who search for free). A smaller, structurally separate value chain sits inside the group: Busy Infotech, a licensed accounting-software vendor to MSMEs.

| Value Chain Stage | Company Role (1 sentence) | Bargaining Power vs Upstream | Bargaining Power vs Downstream | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Platform / marketplace (core, ~92% of consolidated FY26 revenue) | Runs India's largest online B2B classifieds marketplace, taking upfront subscription fees from paying suppliers for placement/lead volume, while buyer access stays free | Strong | Mid | Standalone Revenue from Operations ₹14,428.03 Mn of consolidated ₹15,690.42 Mn in FY26 [FY26 Integrated Annual Report, MD&A, p.83]; largest cost lines are labor and outsourced sales, not a scarce physical input [FY26 Annual Report, Note 21/24] |
| Service provider — content/lead verification & enrichment (upstream input) | Buys third-party data-verification and content-enrichment services rather than owning that function, and runs its own outsourced telesales/channel-partner network to acquire paying suppliers | Strong | n/a | Content development expenses ₹225.86 Mn and Customer support (incl. RFQ/buy-lead verification) ₹628.92 Mn, together ~5.4% of consolidated FY26 revenue [FY26 Annual Report, Note 24]; no vendor named or quantified as a concentrated single source |
| End-customer-facing brand / lead-generation service (to paying suppliers) | Sells MSME suppliers a subscription package (Silver/Gold/Platinum) that substitutes for a sales-and-marketing function they cannot build themselves | n/a | Mid — strong on Gold/Platinum, weak on Silver | "No single customer represents 10% or more of the Group's total revenue" [FY26 Annual Report, Note 33 disclosure, p. — Related Party/Segment note]; Platinum monthly churn <1%, Gold ~1–1.5%, Silver monthly churn ~7% [Q4 FY26 Earnings Call, Apr 30, 2026, transcript] |
| Service provider — accounting/ERP software (Busy Infotech subsidiary, ~8% of consolidated FY26 revenue) | Sells subscription/license-based accounting and ERP software directly to MSME end customers, a separate product and separate value chain from the marketplace | Mid | Mid | Busy Infotech consolidated revenue ₹119 crore (~₹1,190 Mn) FY26, billing ₹170 crore FY26 [Q4 FY26 Earnings Call, Apr 30, 2026, transcript]; not broken out to supplier-concentration or churn detail in this filing |

Bargaining power bands:
- **Strong:** Company sets price, dictates terms, has alternatives
- **Mid:** Negotiated outcomes, no extreme leverage either way
- **Weak:** Price-taker, terms imposed, few alternatives

## 2. Input Cost Pass-Through

There is no commodity or raw-material input to pass through — IndiaMART is an asset-light subscription business with no physical goods in its own cost base, and it states outright that it does not engage in commodity trading, hedging, or exchange-risk management [FY26 Annual Report (Ind AS), Corporate Governance Report — General Shareholder Information]. The dominant cost is labor: consolidated employee benefits expense was ₹6,928.25 Mn in FY26 vs ₹6,009.86 Mn in FY25 (+15% YoY), growing faster than the ~13% consolidated revenue growth over the same period [FY26 Annual Report, Note 21; MD&A p.83]. Outsourced sales cost (the telesales/channel-partner network that signs up new paying suppliers) was ₹800.45 Mn in FY26 vs ₹785.93 Mn in FY25 (+1.8%) [FY26 Annual Report, Note 24]. Because these are wage-linked and services costs, not indexed commodity contracts, there is no contractual escalator or pass-through clause disclosed — the company absorbs wage inflation directly into its P&L, which is the mechanism behind the 284bp standalone EBITDA-margin compression the business-identity read already flagged for FY26.

**Supplier / input concentration (quantify).** The CIQ Suppliers.xls export in the data pool lists ~40 large Indian and multinational industrial, healthcare, and consumer-goods companies (Ajax Engineering, Ashok Leyland, Blue Star, Canon, Cummins India, Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles, and similar) tagged as "Supplier" to IndiaMART — this is a relationship-graph artifact, not a cost-side vendor list: these are large corporates that reference IndiaMART's marketplace in their own filings, not companies IndiaMART sources material inputs from, and none of them appears in the cost notes above with a quantified spend. **Not proven from available data** that IndiaMART discloses a named vendor's share of COGS or purchases, or a single-source/sole-source dependency for any input — the Note 24 "Other expenses" breakdown shows category-level totals (Content development, Internet/hosting, Customer support, Outsourced sales) but no vendor-level concentration, and no risk-factor language in the reviewed filing names a specific third-party dependency (e.g., a named cloud provider or verification vendor) as material. The nearest quantifiable dependency is structural rather than vendor-specific: labor (44% of consolidated FY26 revenue via employee benefits expense alone) is the company's largest and least substitutable input, and it is bought in a competitive, non-concentrated Indian labor market rather than from a single counterparty.

## 3. Customer Pricing Power

IndiaMART can and does raise prices, but the last 24 months show the two customer tiers behave very differently. On the Gold/Platinum side (~50% of paying suppliers, >75% of revenue), pricing power is real: these suppliers buy value-added placement (search targeting, location targeting) that behaves less like a commodity subscription and more like a performance product, and retention stays high (Platinum monthly churn <1%, Gold ~1–1.5%) even as the company raises prices [Q4 FY26 Earnings Call, Apr 30, 2026, transcript]. On the entry-level Silver tier, the evidence points the other way: management implemented a price increase on the Silver subscription tier at the end of Q2 FY26, and by Q4 FY26 attributed roughly 1,000–1,500 of a ~3,000-supplier quarterly shortfall in net additions directly to that price increase (the rest to a geopolitical shock), with Silver monthly churn running ~7% versus ~1% for Platinum [Q4 FY26 Earnings Call, Apr 30, 2026, transcript: "out of that, I would say 1,000, 1,500 could be because of the war, 1,000, 1,500 could have been because of the price"]. Management's own framing — "we are not going back on pricing" despite acknowledging "SMEs are really going through a lot of pain right now" [Q4 FY26 Earnings Call, Apr 30, 2026, transcript] — confirms this was a deliberate price increase that traded near-term Silver-tier volume for higher realized price, not a case of customers simply absorbing it. FY26 ARPU grew 8% (11% for the top decile), but management itself attributes that growth mainly to mix-shift (suppliers upgrading Silver→Gold/Platinum) rather than a base-price increase across the board [FY26 Integrated Annual Report, MD&A, p.82-83], which is consistent with pricing power concentrated at the top of the customer base and weaker at the bottom.

## 4. Economic Control Verdict

**Mixed.**

IndiaMART controls its economics on the supply/input side almost completely — there is no commodity dependency, no disclosed single-vendor concentration, and its largest cost (labor) is bought in a competitive market it can flex up or down through its own sales-force sizing. On the customer side, the picture splits by tier: extreme fragmentation (no customer is 10%+ of revenue) gives IndiaMART structural leverage over any individual paying supplier, and Gold/Platinum customers absorb price increases with low churn — but the Silver tier, roughly half the paying-supplier base by count, pushed back hard enough on a mid-year price increase to cost the company net supplier additions for two consecutive quarters. This is not a squeezed business — no counterparty on either side can dictate terms to IndiaMART — but it is also not full pricing control across the base it serves.

## 5. The Single Biggest Bargaining Risk

The Silver-tier relationship: it is roughly half the paying-supplier base, the most price-sensitive, and the one segment where a proven pricing action has already cost net additions for two straight quarters — if that price resistance spreads to Gold/Platinum (currently insulated by value-added targeting features), the marketplace's core ARPU-growth engine loses its main lever.

# Business Quality — INDIAMART

**Sector overlay applied (fix F-SECTOR-1):** `02_business-identity.md` classifies IndiaMART as an India-focused, subscription-funded B2B online marketplace (classifieds/lead-generation) — no literal row in `frameworks/SECTOR_OVERLAYS.md` matches "online marketplace / classifieds." Business-identity's own §3a judgment call applies the **SaaS / subscription software** row as the nearest functional analog (tiered subscription packages, fees collected upfront and recognised over the contract term, Deferred Revenue as a contract liability, per-account ARPU, and a literal subscription-software subsidiary, Busy Infotech, inside the consolidated group). This overlay is carried forward here: **Repeat/recurring revenue, Margin stability, and Capital intensity use the SaaS-style lens** (Deferred Revenue / billings as the recurring-revenue proxy in the absence of a disclosed NRR figure; GAAP — not adjusted — margin trend; capex/PP&E-light read). The generic 11-factor grammar is used for the remaining factors (pricing power, customer stickiness, competitive intensity, industry rate-of-change, regulatory dependence, commodity dependence, cyclicality, disclosure quality) since no sharper sector-specific lens applies to a marketplace's lead-generation economics.

Upstream inputs used: `02_business-identity.md` (business type), `03_segment-map.md` (REQUIRED, read), `05_customer-geography.md` (REQUIRED, read). Both required upstream files are present — no degraded-confidence flag needed.

## 1. Quality Factor Table

| Quality Factor | Score /100 | Evidence | Comment |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Pricing power *(higher = better)* | 45 | Top-10%-by-ARPU cohort ARPU grew 11% in FY26 vs 8% blended, and management attributes most ARPU growth to suppliers upgrading Silver→Gold/Platinum rather than base-price increases [FY26 Integrated Annual Report, MD&A, p.82-83]. But a Silver-tier price increase in Q4 FY26 directly caused paying-supplier net additions to turn negative that quarter (a decline of 1,200 suppliers) [Q4 FY26 earnings call, Apr 30, 2026, prepared remarks, per `05_customer-geography.md`], and on the Q2 FY26 call management describes actively working to "reduce the competition" faced by suppliers on the platform (i.e., throttling RFQ matches per supplier) rather than raising list price, because doing the latter risks churn [Q2 FY26 earnings call, Oct 17, 2025, Q&A]. | Mixed: real pricing power in the upsell/mix engine (Silver→Gold/Platinum), but demonstrated price elasticity at the entry tier — the company backed off after one Silver increase dented volumes. Not a business that can simply raise price and keep the base. |
| Repeat / recurring revenue *(higher = better; SaaS lens — Deferred Revenue / billings analog)* | 66 | Standalone Deferred Revenue (unearned, already-collected subscription cash) was ₹18,318m at FY26-end, +14% YoY, growing faster than recognised revenue (+9%) [FY26 Integrated Annual Report, MD&A, p.83, per `02_business-identity.md`]. Consolidated contract liabilities were ₹12,202m on the FY26 balance sheet [FY26 Annual Report, Balance Sheet, per `03_segment-map.md`]. But without a disclosed retention number this cannot be scored as durable subscription revenue on par with an enterprise-SaaS book; it is prepaid annual billing with unproven multi-year stickiness. |
| Customer stickiness *(higher = better)* | 40 | No multi-year contracts disclosed; subscriptions renew annually/monthly and cash is "majorly collected in advance for the services to be provided" [FY26 Annual Report (Ind AS), Financial Risk Management — Credit risk, per `05_customer-geography.md`]. Concentration is rising, not falling — top-decile-by-ARPU share of revenue climbed from 41% (FY21) to 49% (FY26) [FY26 Integrated Annual Report, p.83]. Gold+Platinum (~50% of paying suppliers) now generates ~75% of revenue [Q4 FY26 earnings call, Apr 30, 2026]. Switching cost is largely reputational/habitual (buyer familiarity with the platform), not contractual. | Suppliers self-select in and out every renewal cycle with no lock-in; the business retains customers through product value (lead volume) and mix-upgrade momentum, not through switching costs — a materially different (weaker) form of stickiness than a multi-year enterprise contract. |
| Margin stability *(higher = better; SaaS lens — GAAP margin, not non-GAAP)* | 40 | Consolidated GAAP EBITDA margin (CIQ) swung from 39.4% (FY22) → 26.6% (FY23) → 26.5% (FY24) → 37.0% (FY25) → 33.2% (FY26) [Capital IQ Financials Ratios export, FY22–FY26]. Standalone segment EBITDA margin (Note 32) was steadier but still moved 27.4%–40.9% across FY22–FY26 and compressed 284bps in FY26 to 36% as employee/outsourced-sales cost (~49% of standalone revenue) and tech spend outgrew revenue [FY26 Integrated Annual Report, MD&A, p.83, per `02_business-identity.md` and `03_segment-map.md`]. Share-based payment expense roughly doubled YoY (₹347m vs ₹169m, ≈2.4% of standalone revenue) against 9% revenue growth — an SBC-dilution warning consistent with the sector-overlay flag [FY26 Integrated Annual Report, Note 21/Note 28, per `02_business-identity.md`]. Reported Net Income Margin (30–40% in several years per CIQ) is inflated relative to EBITDA margin by treasury/other income on the large IPO-era cash pile, not operating leverage — headline net margin is not a clean read of core-business margin quality. | A double-digit swing in EBITDA margin over five years (26.5% trough to 40.9% peak at the segment level) is not a stable-margin business; the FY26 direction (compressing, cost growth ahead of revenue growth, rising SBC) is also the wrong direction. |

Segment note discloses no material segment capex after FY21 [`03_segment-map.md`, citing Financials (1).xls, Segments tab]. Total Debt/EBITDA is 0.04x and Total Debt/Equity is 0.01x at FY26-end [Capital IQ Financials Ratios export] — the balance sheet carries essentially no leverage funding fixed assets. | A genuinely asset-light platform business — no server/data-center capex burden is visible in the pool, and the shrinking PP&E base likely reflects office-footprint consolidation, not underinvestment in the core product (an inference, not directly evidenced here). |
| Competitive intensity *(low intensity = high score)* | 45 | The company's own risk section names "Competition Risk" (R3) explicitly: "the emergence of new B2B marketplaces, alternative digital commerce platforms, and increasing direct interactions between suppliers and buyers may impact IndiaMART's competitive positioning… could also exert pressure on pricing strategies" [FY26 Integrated Annual Report, Risk Management, R3 Competition Risk, p.2822-2835]. CIQ's competitor list names Amazon.com, Alibaba.com, JioMart, Walmart India, Just Dial, and several vertical/regional B2B platforms as disclosed competitors [Capital IQ Competitors export]. On earnings calls, management repeatedly plays down direct competitive intensity from named peers (e.g., "we haven't heard much about Tradeindia… remains our distantly respected competition" [Q2 FY26 earnings call, Oct 17, 2025]) while separately describing a distinct, internal form of competition — too many suppliers chasing the same buyer RFQ — that the company is actively trying to *reduce* by throttling matches per lead [Q3 FY26 earnings call, Jan 20, 2026; Q2 FY26 earnings call, Oct 17, 2025]. | No large well-funded direct competitor is currently taking share on the calls' own account, but the risk section is not boilerplate — it names direct supplier-buyer disintermediation and new platforms as live threats, and the fact that management must actively manage over-competition *within* its own marketplace (RFQ matching) shows the moat is narrower than "no credible competitor" would suggest. |
| Industry rate-of-change / disruption risk *(low rate-of-change = high score)* | 45 | The core lead-generation-for-MSMEs model has been stable in its basic mechanics for over a decade (subscription tiers, RFQ/Buy-Lead matching), and IndiaMART has held a large registered-supplier base (8.7 million) for years [FY26 Integrated Annual Report, Business Overview, p.81]. But the company is simultaneously layering GenAI/agentic-AI search, WhatsApp-based buyer flows, and a new lending subsidiary (IndiaMART Finance Limited, approved Jul-2026, aimed at supplier working-capital needs) onto the core product [FY26 Integrated Annual Report, p.4335; Key Developments, 2026-07-21]. Management itself frames AI-driven "agentic commerce" and "conversational commerce" as live near-term strategic shifts, not settled ground [FY26 Integrated Annual Report, p.4335]. Buyer discovery increasingly competes with generic search/AI assistants and direct social/WhatsApp channels, a genuinely fast-moving front the company does not control. | Scores in the Weak band (≤40 threshold is close but this sits at 45 — see note below on why the score is not lower). The core subscription/lead-gen mechanic is mature and slow-changing, which is the main reason this does not score in the ≤40 zone; but the discovery layer on top of it (how buyers actually find suppliers — search, AI agents, WhatsApp) is in genuine flux and the winner of that layer is not yet knowable. |
| Regulatory dependence *(low dependence = high score)* | 75 | No sector-specific licensing regime governs a B2B classifieds marketplace the way it governs a bank, telecom, or insurer; the risk section names data-security/compliance frameworks and general corporate/consumer-protection exposure, not an existential regulatory dependency [FY26 Integrated Annual Report, Risk Management section]. The one regulatory-adjacent watch item raised in transcripts is India's government-backed ONDC (Open Network for Digital Commerce) initiative, which one analyst asked about directly as a potential disintermediation threat [Q1 FY23 earnings call, Jul 22, 2022] — a policy-driven infrastructure project, not a licensing constraint, but still a state-directed structural risk to the platform's gatekeeper role. | Low day-to-day regulatory dependence (no license to lose), but a real, named policy-conditional tail risk (ONDC) that could structurally alter how Indian B2B buyer-seller discovery works — this keeps the score out of the 81+ band. |
| Commodity dependence *(low dependence = high score)* | 95 | The business sells subscription access to a software/marketplace platform; it has no input-commodity cost line, no disclosed exposure to a traded commodity price, and no segment or geography note ties revenue or cost to a commodity benchmark [`03_segment-map.md`; `05_customer-geography.md`; no commodity references found in the FY26 Annual Report cost notes reviewed]. | Not proven from available data that any commodity materially drives revenue or cost — essentially commodity-independent, consistent with an asset-light services model. |
| Cyclicality *(low cyclicality = high score)* | 45 | Revenue is a bet on discretionary Indian-MSME marketing/customer-acquisition spend [`05_customer-geography.md`, §4 Read]. FY22–FY26 revenue growth was 12.5%, 30.8%, 21.5%, 16.0%, 13.0% YoY [Capital IQ Financials Ratios export] — decelerating and volatile at the growth-rate level even though never negative in this window, so the trailing five years do not show a full-blown down-cycle. EBITDA growth was far more volatile than revenue growth over the same years (−5.7%, −11.9%, +21.3%, +61.8%, +1.3%) [same source], showing operating leverage cuts both ways and a revenue slowdown would very plausibly turn into a sharper profit slowdown, as it already did in FY23–FY24. Deferred Revenue (subscriptions paid upfront) provides some near-term revenue cushion in a downturn, but does not protect renewal-time demand. | The trailing window is a growth deceleration, not yet a tested recession for this business (IndiaMART has not lived through a full Indian SME-spending downturn as a public, subscription-scale company) — the EBITDA volatility already visible in a merely decelerating environment is the reason this is scored Mixed rather than Strong. |

Gaps exist and are named directly by the segment-map agent: standalone entity discloses no segment split at all, segment capex has not been disclosed since FY21, an "Unallocable" balance-sheet line (₹7,629m, 16.5% of segment assets) is not itemised, and the quantified customer-retention/NRR metric this business's economics turn on is not disclosed anywhere in the reviewed pool [`03_segment-map.md`, §3; `02_business-identity.md`, §3a]. | A clean audit trail and consistent segment structure, but real, specifically-named disclosure gaps (retention/churn, segment capex, standalone segmentation, the unallocable balance-sheet line) on exactly the metrics that would let an outside investor judge recurring-revenue quality — this is why the score sits in the Strong band, not Very Strong. |

## 2. Aggregate Quality Score

**Aggregate: 55/100 (Mixed/Average).**

**Band anchor:** the two lowest row scores are Customer stickiness (40) and Margin stability (40); the aggregate of 55 sits 15 points above the second-lowest row (40), inside the ~20-point ceiling the band anchor requires.

Weighting: Pricing power, Customer stickiness, and Margin stability are given the heaviest weight (roughly 45% combined) because they are the rows where the evidence is most negative and most central to whether this is a durable compounder — a subscription business with no contractual lock-in, rising customer concentration, and a five-year EBITDA-margin range of 26.5%–40.9% is structurally different from a "sticky SaaS" story despite the deferred-revenue growth. Capital intensity and Commodity dependence are weighted lightly (~15% combined) — both are near-ceiling scores, but being asset-light and commodity-free is a baseline feature of this business model, not a differentiator that should pull the aggregate up disproportionately. The remaining rows (recurring revenue, competitive intensity, rate-of-change, regulatory dependence, cyclicality, disclosure quality) sit in the 40–78 range and are weighted at their face value, pulling the blended read toward the middle band.

## 3. Strongest Factor & Weakest Factor

| | Factor | Score | Why |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Strongest | Commodity dependence | 95 | No commodity input or benchmark tie found anywhere in the segment, geography, or cost data reviewed — a structural feature of an asset-light subscription-platform model. |
| Weakest | Customer stickiness / Margin stability (tie) | 40 | No multi-year contracts and rising top-decile revenue concentration (41%→49%, FY21–FY26) on the stickiness side; a five-year EBITDA-margin swing of 26.5%–40.9% with FY26 already compressing 284bps on the margin side — both point to the same underlying weakness, that renewal-time pricing and cost discipline are less protected than the "subscription" label implies. |

## 4. Read

IndiaMART is best read as a dominant, asset-light lead-generation marketplace for Indian MSMEs — not a durable, contractually-locked compounder. The subscription label and growing deferred-revenue book (+14% YoY, ahead of the 9% standalone revenue growth) are genuine positives, but they sit on top of annual/monthly renewals with no disclosed multi-year lock-in, a quantified retention metric that is simply absent from the filings, rising revenue concentration in the top decile of paying suppliers (41%→49% since FY21), and a five-year EBITDA margin range wide enough (26.5%–40.9%) to call "stable" only with real caveats. The single quality factor a buyer should watch over the next 24 months is **customer stickiness / renewal economics** — specifically, whether IndiaMART ever discloses a quantified retention or churn number, and whether the Silver-tier price-elasticity episode seen in Q4 FY26 (a price rise that turned net paying-supplier additions negative) recurs as management tries to keep pushing ARPU. On cyclicality: FY26's ROCE and margin sit closer to a multi-year high than a mid-cycle level — Return on Capital was 15.4% in FY25 and 13.5% in FY26 versus 7.5%–10.3% in FY22–FY24 [Capital IQ Financials Ratios export] — so the currently strong-looking returns are not the through-cycle level; the Cyclicality row (45/100, Mixed) is the more conservative anchor, and a reader should not extrapolate the FY25/FY26 peak margin and ROCE forward without discounting for the EBITDA volatility already visible in a merely decelerating (not recessionary) revenue environment. The industry rate-of-change row scored 45 — inside the Mixed band, not the ≤40 Weak-or-below threshold — so this does **not** trigger the §24 Filter-5 sector/technology-cycle-bet flag; the core subscription mechanic is mature, even though the discovery layer above it (AI search, WhatsApp-based buyer flows, ONDC) is genuinely still in flux and worth monitoring for a future re-score.

## business-model / 08_competitive-map.md

_Source: `business-model/08_competitive-map.md`_

# Competitive Map — INDIAMART

Upstream dependencies check: both required upstream files are present — `02_business-identity.md` and `03_segment-map.md`.

## 1. Dominant Segment

Web and related Services — India's B2B online marketplace connecting buyers and suppliers — is the dominant segment, at 91.96% of FY26 consolidated revenue (₹14,429.38m of ₹15,690.42m) and more than 100% of FY26 segment profit [FY26 Annual Report (Ind AS), Note 32 — Segment information; restated from upstream `03_segment-map.md`].

## 2. Named Competitors

The company's own annual report describes a generic "Competition Risk" — "the emergence of new B2B marketplaces, alternative digital commerce platforms, and increasing direct interactions between suppliers and buyers" — without naming any rival by name [FY26 Integrated Annual Report, Risk Management section, "R3 Competition Risk"]. Specific names come from two other places in the pool: (a) the company's own founder/CEO on quarterly earnings calls, who repeatedly and consistently names the same handful of rivals, and (b) the Capital IQ Competitors export, a mechanically generated list that includes many companies with no real overlap (co-working space operators, study-abroad consultants) alongside the credible ones. This section keeps only names that clear the credibility bar in SELECTION CRITERIA.

### Competitor A — Just Dial Limited

- **Ticker / listing:** NSEI:JUSTDIAL (subsidiary of Reliance Retail Ventures Limited since October 2021) [Capital IQ Competitors export, IndiaMART InterMESH Limited].
- **Where they compete:** India-focused local search and business-listings platform; runs a direct B2B product line ("JD Mart," described by the vendor as "for B2B commerce") that overlaps with IndiaMART's core marketplace [Capital IQ Competitors export, Business Description]. Management itself frames the overlap as partial, not total: "5% to 10% overlap could be with Justdial... on the buyer side as well as on the supplier side" [Q2 FY24 (Oct 2023) earnings call transcript].
- **Scale:** LTM Total Revenue $130.4mm (period ended 2026-06-30, filed 2026-07-10) vs IndiaMART's own LTM Total Revenue of $168.9mm in the same comp run — Just Dial is roughly 0.8x IndiaMART's scale, comfortably inside the 5x credibility band [Capital IQ Quick Comparable Analysis, "Financial Data" tab, IndiaMART InterMESH Limited, as-of 2026-08-13].
- **Profitability / return on capital:** LTM EBITDA margin 29.6% and LTM net income margin 40.5% (the high net margin is inflated by non-operating "other income" — Just Dial carries a large net-cash balance sheet, LTM net debt of −$604.7mm i.e. large net cash) [Capital IQ Quick Comparable Analysis, "Operating Statistics" and "Financial Data" tabs, as-of 2026-08-13]. Return on equity is not cleanly available from this pool; two web aggregators quoted diverging figures on the same day range (ROE ~3.4% per one source, ~8.5%–10.7% per others; ROCE ~7.0%–13.1%) — these are third-party estimates, not filing-sourced, and disagree by a factor of ~3x, so treat the ROE/ROCE figure as directionally low-single-to-low-double-digit but **not precisely pinned down**: Web: Screener.in, 2026-08-13 (unverified); Web: MarketsMojo / Alpha Spread, 2026-07-28 (unverified). The EBITDA/net-margin figures above, sourced to the Capital IQ comp export, are the more reliable anchor for the `moat` agent's peer-margin comparison.
- **Source named in:** Named by the company itself on multiple earnings calls (Q1 FY22, Q2 FY22, Q2 FY24, Q3 FY24, Q2 FY25 transcripts) and appears as a "Named by Company (Self)" entry in the Capital IQ Competitors export.
- **One-line read:** A same-country, comparable-scale rival with a large net-cash balance sheet and a much lower B2B-specific growth trajectory — management's own read is that Just Dial "woke up a little late" on paying-customer growth and IndiaMART moved from 150,000 to nearly 200,000 paying suppliers while Just Dial's numbers stagnated post-COVID [Q2 FY25 (Oct 2024) earnings call transcript].

### Competitor B — TradeIndia (Infocom Network Private Limited)

- **Ticker / listing:** Unlisted / private limited company [Q2 FY24 (Oct 2023) earnings call transcript: "both of them are private limited companies so they file their annual returns with the MCA"].
- **Where they compete:** Identical business model to IndiaMART's core marketplace — a B2B classifieds/lead-generation platform for Indian suppliers and buyers. Management explicitly ranks it, alongside ExportersIndia, as the closest like-for-like rival: "We have always said Trade India and Exporters India are the two which are the nearest one... purely doing the similar business model" [Q2 FY24 (Oct 2023) earnings call transcript].
- **Scale:** Not disclosed in the data pool (private company; MCA annual-return data is referenced by management as something they track internally but the figures themselves are not in this pool). A third-party aggregator estimate puts Infocom Network Private Limited's FY25 (year ended 31 March 2025) revenue in a ₹100–500 crore range (~$12–60mm at typical FX) — a wide, low-confidence range from a non-filing source: Web: RocketReach/Tofler aggregator estimate, 2026 (unverified, wide range, not from an audited filing). On any reading, this is meaningfully smaller than IndiaMART's ~$169mm LTM revenue.
- **Profitability / return on capital:** Not public / not disclosed. No margin or return-on-capital figure for Infocom Network Private Limited exists anywhere in this data pool or in the reliable source tiers.
- **Source named in:** Named directly and repeatedly by the company's own CEO in earnings-call Q&A (Q2 FY24, Q2 FY25 transcripts) as the nearest direct competitor.
- **One-line read:** The company's own most-cited "closest" rival by business-model overlap, but smaller, privately held, and — per management — "no significant change that we have observed from them" [Q2 FY25 (Oct 2024) earnings call transcript], i.e. not viewed internally as a growing threat.

### Competitor C — Alibaba.com / 1688.com (Alibaba Group Holding Limited)

- **Ticker / listing:** NYSE:BABA / HKEX:9988 (Alibaba Group Holding Limited); Alibaba.com Limited itself was taken private by its parent in 2012 and no longer files separately — the Capital IQ Competitors export still carries a stale LTM Revenue figure of $960.05mm dated 2012-03-31, which predates the privatization and should not be used as a current figure [Capital IQ Competitors export, IndiaMART InterMESH Limited].
- **Where they compete:** Global (Alibaba.com) and China-domestic (1688.com) B2B sourcing marketplaces — not a direct India-market competitor for supplier acquisition, but named repeatedly by IndiaMART's own management as the strategic reference point for where the India platform's monetization model could evolve, and as an overlap on the buyer side for cross-border sourcing [Q3 FY24 (Jan 2024) and Q4 FY26 (Apr 2026) earnings call transcripts].
- **Scale:** Management's own estimate, not an Alibaba disclosure: 1688.com has "about 1 million customers and ARPU of about $2,000... that makes it about $2 billion in revenue," built up over roughly 15 years including a phase of "customer-led growth" before shifting toward "ARPU-led growth" once it crossed roughly 750,000 paying sellers [Q4 FY26 (Apr 2026) earnings call transcript]. This is IndiaMART management's own inference about a competitor's business, not a cited Alibaba filing figure — label it accordingly: **Inference, not from filings** (management estimate, unverified against Alibaba's own disclosures). On this estimate, 1688.com's implied revenue is roughly 12x IndiaMART's ~$169mm LTM revenue — well outside the 5x scale band — so this name is included as a strategic/analog reference, not a same-weight-class rival.
- **Profitability / return on capital:** Not public / not disclosed at the 1688.com or Alibaba.com segment level — Alibaba Group Holding reports consolidated and China-Commerce segment results, but does not break out 1688.com's standalone margin or return on capital in the data available here, so no peer figure can be cited for this specific unit.
- **Source named in:** Named directly by the company's own CEO across three separate earnings calls (Q3 FY24, Q2 FY26, Q4 FY26 transcripts) and listed in the Capital IQ Competitors export as a "Named by Company (Self)" entry.
- **One-line read:** Not a same-market rival for supplier acquisition inside India, but the company's own chosen benchmark for what a mature, ARPU-led version of its own subscription model could look like at scale.

## 3. Competitive Position

Position vs peers: **Holding**, based on a proxy rather than disclosed market-share data. IndiaMART does not disclose a market-share percentage in the reviewed filings. The proxy comes from management's own comparative commentary: paying suppliers grew from ~150,000 to ~200,000 over the period cited while Just Dial's paying-customer base "declined for a long period... during... COVID" and only later recovered [Q2 FY25 (Oct 2024) earnings call transcript], and TradeIndia/ExportersIndia showed "no significant change" [same transcript]. Management's own qualitative claim is that current market share is "much higher" than the ~60% it estimates it held at IPO (2019) [Q2 FY24 (Oct 2023) earnings call transcript] — this is a company-sourced, unverified claim (Level 3, transcript) with no independent confirmation in this pool, so it should not be read as more than directional. Set against that read, the company's own most recent disclosed metric shows paying-supplier growth decelerating sharply — 220,000 in FY26 vs 217,000 in FY25, +1.4% YoY, well below the 8% five-year CAGR since FY21 [FY26 Integrated Annual Report, MD&A, p.82-83, cited in upstream `02_business-identity.md`] — which tempers a clean "gaining" read; "Holding" better reflects a business that is not visibly losing named-competitor customers but whose own growth engine has slowed.

## 4. Competitive Shape

The credible competitive set in India's B2B marketplace/classifieds segment is small and asymmetric: one comparable-scale public rival (Just Dial, via its JD Mart product) whose core business is local search rather than pure B2B marketplace; a smaller pure-play private direct competitor (TradeIndia/Infocom Network) that management itself has watched for years without observing material share shifts; and diffuse, partial (5–10%) overlap with horizontal platforms (Google, Amazon, and separately Meta properties) that management names as the four or five places SME advertising spend actually competes for attention [Q3 FY24 (Jan 2024) earnings call transcript: "there are only 4, 5 large platforms... between IndiaMART and Google and Amazon and Justdial... And Facebook and WhatsApp and Instagram"]. No HHI or independent third-party market-share dataset exists in this pool. Read together, this is closer to a **concentrated few-firm segment with one dominant player** (IndiaMART, on management's own unverified ~60%-plus estimate) than a fragmented market with many equal-sized rivals — but that read rests on a single company-sourced claim, not an audited or third-party share survey, and should be treated as directional only.

## 5. Caveat

Two limitations should be carried forward to `moat`:
1. **No independently audited or third-party market-share data exists in this pool.** Every share and "position vs peers" claim in Section 3 traces back to IndiaMART's own management commentary on earnings calls — useful as the company's internal view, but not corroborated by an external source (e.g., an independent industry report or a competitor's own disclosed customer count).
2. **TradeIndia/Infocom Network — the competitor management itself calls "nearest"** — discloses no public financials in this pool; its scale/margin data above rests on a wide, low-confidence third-party web estimate, not a filing. If a future data pull can obtain Infocom Network's MCA-filed annual return (referenced by management as something the company tracks internally), that would materially sharpen the closest same-business-model comparison.

# Moat — INDIAMART

Upstream dependency check: `08_competitive-map.md` (REQUIRED) is present — named competitors below are inherited from it, none added. `07_business-quality.md` and `10_external-dependency.md` (both OPTIONAL) are present and read for the cyclicality/rate-of-change cross-checks used in the economic-moat test and the trajectory call.

## 1. Named Competitors

(Inherited verbatim from `08_competitive-map.md` §2 — no new names added here.)

- **Just Dial Limited (NSEI:JUSTDIAL)** — India-focused local-search platform with a direct B2B product line (JD Mart); management estimates only 5–10% buyer/supplier overlap; roughly 0.8x IndiaMART's scale on LTM revenue; large net-cash balance sheet.
- **TradeIndia (Infocom Network Private Limited)** — Unlisted, private; management's own repeatedly named "nearest" like-for-like rival (identical classifieds/lead-gen model); smaller, no public financials.
- **Alibaba.com / 1688.com (Alibaba Group Holding Limited)** — Global/China-domestic B2B sourcing marketplaces; not a same-market India rival for supplier acquisition, but management's own chosen strategic benchmark for a mature, ARPU-led subscription model; ~12x IndiaMART's scale on management's own (unverified) estimate — included as a strategic reference, not a same-weight-class competitor.

## 2. Moat Sources

| Possible Moat | Present? (Y/N) | Evidence | Strength /100 |
|---|---|---|---:|
| Brand | Y (weak-to-mixed) | Self-described "India's largest" online B2B marketplace with 230 million registered buyers and 8.7 million registered suppliers across 98,000 categories [FY26 Integrated Annual Report, Business Overview, p.81, per `02_business-identity.md`]. Management's own claim that current share is "much higher" than the ~60% it estimates it held at IPO is company-sourced and unverified — no independent brand-tracking, awareness survey, or third-party share dataset exists in this pool [Q2 FY24 (Oct 2023) earnings call transcript, per `08_competitive-map.md` §3, Caveat §5.1]. | 42 |
| Cost advantage | N | No disclosed unit-cost comparison vs named peers exists in the pool. IndiaMART's EBIT margin (32.0% LTM) is higher than Just Dial's (25.3% LTM) [Company Comparable Analysis, Operating Statistics tab, as-of 2026-08-13], but that gap reflects a different business mix (pure B2B subscription vs Just Dial's broader local-search product), not a proven structural cost edge — **not proven from available data** that IndiaMART buys or produces its core service more cheaply than a named competitor. | 20 |
| Distribution | Y (mixed) | Nationwide sales-and-service network across 1,000+ cities, ~5,376-person sales/customer-service organisation and an outsourced telesales/channel-partner layer used to acquire and service paying suppliers [FY26 Integrated Annual Report, MD&A, p.82, per `02_business-identity.md`; `06_value-chain.md` §2]. This is real, disclosed infrastructure that a small private rival (TradeIndia) is unlikely to match at the same scale, per management's own framing of TradeIndia as having shown "no significant change" for years [Q2 FY25 (Oct 2024) earnings call transcript]. The advantage is muted against Just Dial, which runs a comparable local-sales-force model at roughly 0.8x IndiaMART's revenue scale. | 52 |
| Scale | Y (mixed) | 8.7 million registered suppliers, 230 million registered buyers, 220,000 paying suppliers, 129 million listings [FY26 Integrated Annual Report, Business Overview, p.81]. Clear scale gap vs TradeIndia (small, private, no disclosed financials — the closest same-business-model rival by management's own account, but not shown to be a growing threat) [`08_competitive-map.md` §2, Competitor B]. Scale is comparable, not dominant, vs Just Dial on revenue (0.8x) [`08_competitive-map.md` §2, Competitor A]. | 55 |
| Technology / IP | N | No patent, proprietary-algorithm, or licensed-technology disclosure found in the business overview, MD&A, or risk section reviewed. The company is layering GenAI/agentic search and WhatsApp-based flows onto the core product, but frames these as live strategic bets, not a proprietary technology edge already built and defensible [FY26 Integrated Annual Report, p.4335, per `07_business-quality.md`]. **Not proven from available data.** | 18 |
| Licenses / regulation | N | No sector-specific license governs a B2B classifieds marketplace, unlike a bank, telecom, or insurer [`10_external-dependency.md` §1, "Regulation" row; `07_business-quality.md`, Regulatory dependence row, scored 75/100 = low dependence]. A low-dependence read is the opposite of a licensing moat — there is no barrier here that keeps a well-funded new entrant out. | 10 |
| Network effects | Y (present, congestion-limited) | Classic two-sided marketplace mechanics — a larger buyer base (230 million registered) makes the platform more valuable to suppliers, and a larger supplier base makes it more valuable to buyers. But management is simultaneously working to actively *reduce* competition among suppliers on the platform by throttling RFQ/lead matches per supplier, describing this as a deliberate lever [Q2 FY26 earnings call, Oct 17, 2025, Q&A, per `07_business-quality.md`, Competitive intensity row] — i.e., the network effect has a proven congestion problem (too many suppliers chasing the same buyer lead dilutes the value each supplier receives) that requires active management, not a self-reinforcing virtuous cycle running unmanaged. | 48 |

The Silver-tier price increase in Q4 FY26 directly turned net paying-supplier additions negative that quarter — direct, real-time proof that a meaningful share of the customer base will leave rather than absorb a price rise, the opposite of a switching-cost moat [Q4 FY26 earnings call, Apr 30, 2026, per `04_unit-economics.md` §4]. | 28 |

No single moat source clears the Strong band (61–80) on its own; the strongest reads (Distribution, Scale, Network effects) sit in the Mixed band (41–60), each with a named, evidenced limitation (muted vs Just Dial, congestion-managed, no independent share data).

## 3. Competitive Economics

| Company / Competitor | Gross Margin | EBIT Margin | Return on capital (ROIC, or ROE for financials) | Period | Source |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| IndiaMART (operating company — ROIC lens) | 55.6% (LTM, CIQ comps basis) / 76% (FY26 standalone, Revenue − Customer Service Cost basis) | 32.0% (LTM) | 13.51% (FY26); 5-yr avg (FY22–FY26) **11.23%**; LTM (Jun-26) 14.92% | LTM as-of 2026-08-13 / FY26 (ended 31 Mar 2026) | Gross/EBIT margin: [Company Comparable Analysis, Operating Statistics tab, as-of 2026-08-13]; standalone gross margin: [FY26 Annual Report, p.82, "Financial Overview – Standalone", per `04_unit-economics.md`]; Return on Capital %: [Capital IQ Financials (1).xls, Ratios tab, FY22–FY26 + LTM] |
| Competitor 1 — Just Dial Limited (NSEI:JUSTDIAL) | 39.9% (LTM) | 25.3% (LTM) | ROE ~3.4%–10.7%, ROCE ~7.0%–13.1% (wide, third-party web estimates, not filing-sourced — **not precisely pinned down**) | LTM as-of 2026-08-13 | Margin figures: [Company Comparable Analysis, Operating Statistics tab, as-of 2026-08-13] — reused from `08_competitive-map.md` §2, Competitor A per that agent's own instruction not to re-pull a figure it already sourced; ROE/ROCE: Web: Screener.in, 2026-08-13 (unverified); Web: MarketsMojo/Alpha Spread, 2026-07-28 (unverified), as cited in `08_competitive-map.md` §2 |
| Competitor 2 — TradeIndia (Infocom Network Private Limited) | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | — | Private company; no public financials in this pool [`08_competitive-map.md` §2, Competitor B] |
| Competitor 3 — Alibaba.com / 1688.com (Alibaba Group Holding Limited) | Not disclosed at segment level | Not disclosed at segment level | Not disclosed at segment level | — | Alibaba Group reports consolidated/China-Commerce segment results only; 1688.com standalone margin/return is not broken out [`08_competitive-map.md` §2, Competitor C] |

**Cross-check of the headline return figure (required by CLAUDE.md §15/§21 hygiene).** The table above uses Capital IQ's own "Return on Capital %" line as the primary figure. A hand-computed cross-check on the standard base (NOPAT ÷ average invested capital) for FY26, using **EBIT ₹5,015.93m** [Capital IQ Financials (1).xls, Income Statement tab] and the **normalized structural tax rate of 25.17%** (India's statutory corporate tax rate for domestic companies, per the FY26 Note 26 tax reconciliation — see below) against **average Total Capital (debt + equity) of ₹23,323.5m** (FY25 ₹24,234.77m and FY26 ₹22,412.26m) [Capital IQ Financials (1).xls, Capital Structure Summary tab], gives: NOPAT = 5,015.93 × (1 − 0.2517) = ₹3,753.4m; ROIC = 3,753.4 / 23,323.5 = **16.1%** — about 258 basis points (bps — hundredths of a percentage point) above CIQ's own reported 13.51% for FY26. This is a material divergence and is flagged, not silently resolved: it most likely reflects a different capital-base definition or averaging convention inside Capital IQ's proprietary "Return on Capital %" methodology that cannot be fully reconstructed from the disclosed export. Per the source hierarchy and the conservative default (CLAUDE.md §4), **this report uses the lower, vendor-reported CIQ figure (13.51% FY26 / 11.23% five-year average) as the primary anchor**, not the higher hand-computed 16.1%.

**Normalized tax rate, stated.** FY26's reported effective tax rate was 26.74%, up from 21.98% in FY25 [FY26 Annual Report (Ind AS), Note 26(c) — Reconciliation of tax expense]. The company's own reconciliation shows this is driven mainly by (i) a shrinking benefit from income taxed at lower rates (₹152.38m in FY26 vs ₹368.14m in FY25) and (ii) rising business losses at loss-making consolidated subsidiaries (Busy Infotech/Livekeeping) for which no deferred tax asset is recognised (₹206.99m in FY26 vs ₹167.27m in FY25) — both structural/subsidiary-consolidation effects, not core-marketplace operating economics. The **statutory rate of 25.17%** [FY26 Annual Report (Ind AS), Note 26(c)] is used here as the normalized structural rate — it sits close to the 5-year average reported effective rate (~24.5%: 23.77%, 23.55%, 26.50%, 21.98%, 26.74% for FY22–FY26) [Capital IQ, Income Statement tab] and strips out the subsidiary-consolidation and rate-mix noise that pushed FY26's reported rate above trend. This rate is the anchor for any downstream DCF (`valuation/04_intrinsic-dcf`) reconciling to the same normalized NOPAT base.

**Through-cycle, not peak-year.** `07_business-quality.md` (§4, Read) already flags FY25/FY26 as sitting near a multi-year high — Return on Capital was 15.40% (FY25) and 13.51% (FY26) vs 7.46%–10.26% in FY22–FY24 [Capital IQ, Ratios tab, cross-checked against the same figures cited in `07_business-quality.md`]. The single-year FY26 figure is therefore labelled a **near-peak year, not the through-cycle level**; the 5-year average of 11.23% is used for the economic-moat test below.

**Net-cash structure — gross-capital basis shown, net-of-cash not meaningful.** IndiaMART is a net-cash company: FY26 Total Cash & Short-Term Investments were ₹33,886.58m against Total Capital (debt + equity) of only ₹22,412.26m [Capital IQ Financials (1).xls, Capital Structure Summary tab] — cash and near-cash investments exceed the entire debt-plus-equity capital base. A net-of-cash invested-capital figure would therefore be **negative** (₹22,412.26m − ₹33,886.58m = −₹11,474.32m for FY26; also negative in FY25), making a net-of-cash ROIC mathematically undefined/not meaningful. The gross-capital basis (CIQ's reported "Return on Capital %," debt + equity, cash not netted) is therefore the only usable basis and is what is used throughout this section — it is already the more conservative of the two possible readings, since netting out the large cash pile would (if it produced a positive denominator) mechanically inflate the ratio.

**The economic moat test (required).**

> Return on capital **above** cost of capital, on the base-case estimate — but the margin is thin and not robust to a plausible change in the cost-of-capital assumption: **11.23% 5-yr avg ROIC (gross-capital basis)** vs **≈8.75% estimated WACC** (+~248 bps) — [CAPM estimate, inputs shown below; **Inference, not from filings**].

- **Cost-of-capital sourcing (priority per CLAUDE.md §4/report structure).** No company-disclosed WACC, cost of equity, or hurdle rate exists anywhere in the reviewed filings or transcripts. A CAPM estimate is therefore built and labelled as inference: risk-free rate = 6.85% (India 10-year G-Sec yield, ~Jul–Aug 2026) [Web: BusinessToday, 2026-08-05, "10 year G Sec yield climbs to 6.85% in July" — dated, unverified]; equity risk premium (India) = 7.31% [Web: Damodaran country equity-risk-premium dataset, July 2026 update — dated, unverified]; beta (5-year) = 0.26 [Capital IQ Public Company Profile export; corroborated independently in Company Comparable Analysis, Operating Statistics tab, as-of 2026-08-13]. Cost of equity = 6.85% + 0.26 × 7.31% = **8.75%**. Because Total Debt/Capital is only ~0.97% at FY26-end [Capital IQ Financials (1).xls, Ratios tab], WACC ≈ cost of equity ≈ **8.75–8.8%** — debt is too small to move the blended figure meaningfully.
- **Flagged sensitivity — the beta input is unusually low and the test is not robust to it.** A 5-year beta of 0.26 is low for a mid-cap, India-only, still-decelerating-growth internet/marketplace stock; more conventional betas used for comparable small/mid-cap growth internet names (roughly 0.8–1.0) would push the CAPM cost of equity to **≈12.7%–14.2%**. Under that more conventional assumption, the 5-year average ROIC of 11.23% would sit **at or below** the cost of capital, not above it — and even on the low-beta base case, one trough year in the window (FY23, ROIC 7.46%) already sits below the CAPM estimate. This sensitivity is material enough that the "above cost of capital" read cannot be treated as robust, and it is the deciding factor capping the verdict below Strong in §5.

## 4. Where The Company Sits

1. **Relative to peers.** Company sits at or near the **top** of the two named peers with disclosed financial data on operating margin — IndiaMART's LTM EBIT margin (32.0%) and gross margin (55.6%) both exceed Just Dial's (25.3% EBIT, 39.9% gross) [Company Comparable Analysis, Operating Statistics tab, as-of 2026-08-13]. On net income margin, Just Dial is higher (40.5% vs 30.6%), but that is driven by Just Dial's large net-cash treasury income (non-operating), the same distortion `08_competitive-map.md` §2 flags for that company — it does not reflect a superior core-marketplace business. A clean return-on-capital comparison against Just Dial is not possible: the only Just Dial figures available are wide, unverified web-aggregator ROE/ROCE ranges (3.4%–13.1%), not a filing-sourced, comparably-defined ROIC. TradeIndia and 1688.com/Alibaba.com disclose no comparable margin or return data at all. **Insufficient data to make a precise, filing-grade return-on-capital comparison against named peers**, though the operating-margin comparison against Just Dial is directionally favorable to IndiaMART.
2. **Absolute (the economic moat test).** IndiaMART earns a return on capital **modestly above** its estimated cost of capital on the base-case, low-beta CAPM estimate (11.23% 5-yr avg ROIC vs ≈8.75% WACC, +~248 bps) — but this result flips to **at or below** cost of capital under a more conventional beta assumption for a comparable small/mid-cap Indian internet stock (implying a ≈12.7%–14.2% WACC). The test is **not robustly assessable as "above"** given this sensitivity; it is closer to a borderline pass than a clear one.

## 5. Moat Verdict

**Narrow moat.**

The strongest evidenced advantages are Distribution and Scale relative to the closest true same-business-model rival, TradeIndia (a private, small competitor management itself has watched for years without observing material share shifts), plus a real but congestion-limited two-sided network effect. None of these clears the Strong band on its own, and the decisive economic test — return on capital versus cost of capital — passes only on a base-case CAPM estimate built on an unusually low disclosed beta (0.26); under a more conventional beta for a comparable small/mid-cap growth internet name, the 5-year average ROIC (11.23%) would sit at or below the estimated cost of capital, and even the base case shows a trough year (FY23) already below it. Combined with proven-weak switching costs (no contractual lock-in; a Silver-tier price rise in Q4 FY26 directly turned net supplier additions negative) and margin instability (EBITDA margin ranged 26.5%–40.9% over five years, per `07_business-quality.md`), this is a company with real, if partial, structural advantages over its named competitors that produce economics *close to* — not durably and robustly above — its cost of capital. The five-year test this moat would need to pass: sustaining a return on capital clearly and robustly above a properly-estimated cost of capital (not one resting on a fragile low-beta assumption) while the AI-search/agentic-commerce discovery layer above the core subscription mechanic — which `07_business-quality.md` itself flags as genuinely still in flux — plays out.

**Moat trajectory: stable, with a specific near-term erosion warning.** The 5-year return-on-capital trend is not falling — it rose from 10.26% (FY22) to a 15.40% peak (FY25) before easing to 13.51% (FY26) [Capital IQ, Ratios tab] — and `08_competitive-map.md`'s own competitive-position read is "Holding" (not clearly gaining or losing share against the named peers), based on management's own account that TradeIndia shows "no significant change" and Just Dial's paying-customer base only recently recovered from a COVID-era decline. That supports "stable" over "eroding" as the level call. But three specific, evidenced signals point toward erosion risk if they continue: (1) paying-supplier net additions turned negative in three of the last four disclosed quarters (Q3 FY26 −1,000, Q4 FY26 −1,200, Q1 FY27 −1,850) against an 8% five-year CAGR, tied directly to a Silver-tier price increase and a geopolitical shock [`04_unit-economics.md` §2–§4]; (2) standalone EBITDA margin compressed 284 bps in FY26 as employee/outsourced-sales cost and tech spend outgrew revenue [`07_business-quality.md`, Margin stability row]; and (3) the industry rate-of-change score sits in the Mixed band (45/100) specifically because the buyer-discovery layer (GenAI search, WhatsApp flows, ONDC) is named by management itself as genuinely unsettled [`07_business-quality.md`, Industry rate-of-change row]. None of these yet forces an "eroding" call on the data available, but they are the concrete triggers that would flip this call at the next re-score, and — per CLAUDE.md §24 Filter 5 — durability should be discounted accordingly given the discovery-layer instability sitting on top of an otherwise mature core mechanic.

This is a live, named external shock moving subscriber adds/losses, not a hypothetical risk-factor line. | [Q4 FY26 Earnings Call, Apr 30, 2026, transcript: "It took longer than we expected, especially in the March when the war also broke out... I think if there was no war, we could have been probably 2,000 customers positive... out of that, I would say 1,000, 1,500 could be because of the war"]; [Q4 FY26 Earnings Call, Apr 30, 2026: "it is taking much longer given the geopolitical as well as the pricing because SMEs are really going through a lot of pain right now"]; [Q1 FY27 Earnings Call, Jul 21, 2026: "whether it is to do with our own or whether it is to do with traffic migrating to LLM or whether it is to do with the war and U.S. tension, I can't really tell"] |
| Consumer cycle | High | The subscriber base is India's SME/MSME sector, and management's own risk register names this explicitly: "R1 Economic Risk — Sudden shifts in the macroeconomic environment... can significantly influence economic conditions, market dynamics, and business confidence and investment decisions." On the same Q4 FY26 call, management said price increases were landing badly "because SMEs are really going through a lot of pain right now," and paying-supplier net-additions and collection growth have both decelerated over FY26 (collection growth cited as slowing quarter over quarter in the Q3 FY26 call). Because paying-subscriber willingness to spend on a discretionary lead-generation subscription tracks SME cash-flow health, this is close to the single biggest swing factor in near-term results. | [FY26 Integrated Annual Report, Risk Management — "R1 Economic Risk"]; [Q4 FY26 Earnings Call, Apr 30, 2026: "SMEs are really going through a lot of pain right now"]; [Q3 FY26 Earnings Call, Jan 20, 2026: "you see this particular quarter, we have reversed from a sub-10% growth... a bit of a slowdown. In Q1 FY'26, it was 9% growth, 7% last quarter, it's come down to 6%"] |
| Industrial cycle | Mid | IndiaMART's supplier base spans manufacturing, industrial plants/machinery, construction, and engineering categories (listed among its ~57 industries/98,000 categories), so a broader India industrial slowdown would hit supplier demand to advertise/list. But the platform mix is broader than pure industrials — consumer goods, healthcare supplies, agricultural products, and services categories are also large — so this is a partial, not dominant, channel, and it overlaps heavily with the "Consumer cycle" (SME sentiment) row above rather than being a distinct commodity-driven industrial-capex cycle. | [FY26 Integrated Annual Report — category list: "Construction & Building, Industrial Plants, Machinery, Construction Machinery... to consumer goods, healthcare supplies and agricultural products, IndiaMART..."] |

## 2. Sensitivity, If Disclosed

| Variable | Disclosed Sensitivity | Basis | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Investment portfolio NAV (proxy for interest-rate / market-price risk on treasury book) | +5% NAV move on mutual funds, ETFs, bonds, debentures → +₹1,426.29 million impact on profit before tax (FY26); −5% → −₹1,426.29 million | FY26 (year ended 31 March 2026); FY25 comparative: ±₹1,320.13 million | [FY26 Annual Report (Ind AS), Note 31 — Financial risk management objectives and policies, Interest rate risk sensitivity table] |
| Foreign-currency exposure | Company states unhedged FX exposure "is not material" as at 31 March 2026 and 31 March 2025 — no numeric sensitivity given because the exposure (US-dollar trade receivables) is small | FY26 / FY25 | [FY26 Annual Report (Ind AS), Note 31(a) Foreign currency risk] |
| Commodity price / FX hedging | None disclosed — company states it does not engage in commodity trading, hedging, or exchange-risk management activities | Current | [FY26 Annual Report (Ind AS), Corporate Governance Report — General Shareholder Information item (h)] |

No sector-cyclicality sensitivity table (e.g., "a 100bp move in India GDP growth changes billings by X%") is disclosed anywhere in the pool; the SME-demand link is qualitative (management commentary, cited in Section 1), not quantified by the company.

## 3. Classification

**Partly externally driven.**

The balance-sheet-level external exposures (FX, commodity, freight, weather, interest rate on debt) are genuinely small or not applicable — this is a debt-free (Total Debt/EBITDA ~0.04x), 99.6%-India-revenue, asset-light subscription business with no commodity input and no hedging program because it needs none [Financials-1 Capital-Structure-Details.xls; Financials.xls Segments tab]. That is the "company-controlled" half of the picture: pricing, product mix (Silver/Gold/Platinum tiers), sales-force allocation, and the accounting-software bolt-on (Busy, Vyapar) are levers management pulls directly.

But the demand side is a different story. Paying-supplier additions and collection growth are visibly exposed to two forces management does not control: (1) the health of India's SME sector — management's own risk register names "Economic Risk" first among six standing risks, and on two consecutive earnings calls (Q4 FY26, Q1 FY27) leadership directly blamed weak net adds and buyer inquiries on SME financial pain, a geopolitical "war" event, and India-U.S. tension, rather than on execution; and (2) government MSME/GST policy, which the MD&A itself frames as the tailwind underpinning its addressable market (Udyam-registered enterprises grew from 7.9 million in FY22 to 79.4 million in FY26 largely on the back of formalization policy, not IndiaMART's own actions) [FY26 Integrated Annual Report, MD&A]. Because pricing power, retention programs, and product bundling are real, proven management levers that operate on top of — and can partly offset — these forces, this is not a pure pass-through name; it sits in the "material exposure with real levers" band.

## 4. External Dependency Risk Score

**52/100 — inverted scale: higher = worse (more dangerous external dependence).**

Drivers of the score: two High-dependency rows (Geopolitics, Consumer/SME cycle) and one Mid-dependency row with a real earnings swing (Interest rate/investment NAV, ~27% of FY26 EBITDA at a 5% NAV move) pull the score up from the "company-controlled" floor. It stays out of the 61+ band because FX, commodity, freight, and weather are genuinely not applicable or immaterial, debt-linked rate risk is negligible, and management demonstrably has and uses direct levers (pricing, subscriber tiering, product bundling) that the transcripts show working even through the SME-pain and geopolitical-shock quarters (paid subscriber base and revenue both kept growing through FY26 even as net adds slowed).

## 5. The Single Biggest Lever

A 20% adverse move in India SME/MSME sentiment and spending capacity — the "Consumer cycle" row — would do the most damage: it is the demand-side variable management has already named as the cause of decelerating collection growth and net-subscriber losses over FY26–FY27, it cannot be hedged or offset with a financial instrument the way currency or rate risk can, and it hits the core subscription-renewal engine directly rather than the smaller treasury-income line.

## 2. Classification

**Capital allocation concerns.** The balance sheet is debt-free with net cash of roughly ₹31bn (FY26), working capital is structurally negative (customers pay upfront, no inventory), dividends are well covered, and the auditor, related-party, and board-process signals are individually clean or only mildly flagged. The one specific, recurring issue with how capital is spent is the pattern of deploying cash into a wide portfolio of small minority stakes in unrelated startups (fleet management, HR SaaS, legal tech, procurement, accounting software) on top of one sizeable control acquisition (Busy Infotech, $66.93mm) — a serial pattern with a mixed track record (one acquired subsidiary, Livekeeping Private Limited, was struck off in October 2024; Ten Times Online was divested in 2023 for a nominal $0.01mm after being bought for a nominal sum in 2020; a ₹23.81mn impairment and a ₹12.04mn diminution provision were both recorded against these investments in FY2025). This is the specific capital-allocation issue, set against otherwise clean governance.

## 3. Most Material Signal

The acquisition pattern is the single signal that would change this classification if it deteriorated further. Today the deals are individually small (mostly single-digit-to-low-double-digit-million-dollar minority checks), entirely self-funded from operating cash flow with zero debt drawn, and the one control deal (Busy Infotech, ~5% of the company's own ~$1.3bn equity value [Public Ownership Summary — market value ₹107,319.4mn at ₹1,784.21/share, Aug-11-2026]) is not large relative to the company's own value — so the acquisition-pattern row is scored 58/100, below the ≥70 threshold that would trigger the rejector-filter cap under CLAUDE.md §24 / Filter 4. If the company began funding deals with debt, wrote off a larger share of the roughly $250–300mm cumulative amount committed to this venture portfolio over ten years, or made a control acquisition priced near or above its own market value, this row would cross into serial-acquirer disqualifier territory and cap the Capital Allocation Score at 50/100 regardless of the otherwise clean balance sheet and governance signals.

## 4. Capital Allocation Score /100

**74/100.**

The ≥70-severity rejector-filter cap (CLAUDE.md §24, Filter 4) is **not applied**: the acquisition-pattern row scored 58/100 — a genuine serial pattern of deal-making that keeps this score out of the "very strong" band, but not the debt-funded, near-or-above-company-value pattern the cap is designed for. The 74/100 reflects a debt-free balance sheet with net cash as a strategic asset, unqualified audits back to at least FY2015, small and mostly disclosed-as-immaterial related-party transactions, stable and high founder ownership (~49%), well-covered and growing dividends, and structurally negative working capital — offset against the recurring minority-stake venture investing (opportunity cost of capital and management attention spread across ~15+ small, largely unproven positions, several with write-downs or exits at a loss), one procedural share-pledge compliance lapse by an unnamed Designated Person, a related-party "office or place of profit" appointment that drew 21.7% shareholder dissent, and board/CFO turnover concentrated in the last two years.

Filing regime: India — SEBI LODR + Companies Act 2013, Ind AS, INR, fiscal year ends March 31 [FY26 Integrated Annual Report (Jun-02-2026 filing)]. All six upstream specialist outputs are present in the pool; no upstream gap note is required.

## 2. New Red Flags

| Red Flag | Why It Matters | Evidence | Severity /100 *(higher = worse)* |
|---|---|---|---:|
| Buyer-side funnel stagnation, admitted by management | IndiaMART's economics depend on a two-sided network: paying suppliers renew because buyer-generated leads (RFQs) are valuable. Management directly confirmed the buyer count is stagnating/declining organically — a leading indicator for future lead volume and, eventually, supplier willingness to renew or upgrade — that neither `customer-geography` (which covers only the paying-supplier side) nor `business-quality`'s rate-of-change row (which frames buyer-discovery risk as a future AI/search threat, not an already-observed decline) captured directly. | Q1 FY27 earnings call, Jul 21, 2026, Q&A: analyst asks about "number of buyers on our platform going down"; CEO response: "while on a overall number, you are seeing that the overall number of buyers are stagnating... On the overall decline of the buyer, because currently we are experimenting more with Google, and since our primary source of new buyer acquisition..." and confirms the company deliberately "did cut down on some of the non-quality buyers" via reduced advertising spend (down to "8 crores per quarter") over the prior "4, 5 quarters" [IndiaMART InterMESH Limited, Q1 2027 Earnings Call, Jul 21, 2026, Q&A] | 55 |

Management states the initial design is a partnership-lending model, not balance-sheet lending, but a new subsidiary in "Financial Services" is a strategic-scope expansion that neither `segment-map` (which covers only the two existing reported segments) nor `capital-allocation-governance`'s acquisition-pattern row (which covers past deals, not this newly incorporated entity) addresses. | Key Developments, 2026-07-21: Board approved incorporation of "IndiaMART Finance Limited," industry classified "Financial Services," objective "to strengthen trust, engagement and retention of the users on the platform by enabling such business users primarily to meet their short term working capital requirements/financial needs," paid-up capital ₹0.5mn (50,000 equity shares of ₹10 each), 100% subsidiary [Key Developments.xls; Corporate Timeline.xls]; incorporated Aug 4, 2026 [Key Developments.xls, 2026-08-04]; CEO on Q1 FY27 call, Jul 21, 2026: "We do not have any plans to lend out of our own balance sheet any large amount. It is mainly to do the partnerships and short-term financing" [Q1 FY27 Earnings Call, Jul 21, 2026, Q&A] | 40 |

| Gratuity (defined-benefit) plan underfunded | The Group's defined-benefit obligation (₹827.66mn at FY26-end) exceeds plan assets (₹236.58mn) by roughly ₹591mn — a funded-status gap of about 71% of the obligation. This is immaterial next to total equity (~₹24bn) and was not addressed by any upstream report (no upstream agent's scope covers the Pension/OPEB note). | [IndiaMART InterMESH Limited NSEI:INDIAMART Financials (1).xls, Pension/OPEB tab — Proj. Benefit Obligation (Pension) ₹827.66mn, Total Plan Assets ₹236.58mn, FY ended Mar-31-2026] | 15 |

## 3. Most Severe New Flag

The most material new flag is the **buyer-side funnel stagnation management confirmed on the Q1 FY27 call**. IndiaMART's entire subscription-renewal economics — the ~75% of revenue sitting with the Gold/Platinum cohort that `customer-geography` and `business-quality` both flag as the core dependency — rest on suppliers continuing to see enough buyer-generated leads to justify renewing and upgrading. Management's own words ("the overall number of buyers are stagnating") describe the demand side of the marketplace, the side no other specialist report examines directly, going flat at the same time the company is deliberately cutting advertising spend and re-routing acquisition channels away from an underperforming source. If buyer volume keeps stagnating while supplier renewal pricing keeps rising (per `business-quality`'s Silver-tier price-elasticity finding), the two effects compound: fewer leads per supplier at a higher price, which is the precise mechanism that would eventually show up as slower paying-supplier net adds or falling ARPU-tier upgrades. This is a leading indicator the synthesizer should weight alongside — not instead of — the already-flagged supplier-concentration and margin-volatility findings.

## 4. Cross-Cutting Patterns

Three findings point the same direction: management is spreading capital and attention away from the core marketplace at the exact moment the core marketplace shows its first demand-side softening. The buyer funnel is stagnating (this report, Section 2), the Accounting Software Services segment is still loss-making in 3 of the last 4 years (`segment-map`), the Vyapar associate is generating a growing net loss (`segment-map`, −₹547.72mn in FY26), and the company just added a fourth active initiative — a financial-services subsidiary — on top of an already-serial pattern of ~19 minority venture-style deals (`capital-allocation-governance`). None of these individually crosses a hard threshold, but together they describe a company diversifying its management bandwidth into unrelated or early-stage lines while the flagship subscription funnel it depends on for ~92% of revenue (`segment-map`) is showing its first buyer-side deceleration in the trailing quarters reviewed.

# Earnings Module — INDIAMART (Synthesis)

## Abstract

IndiaMART's earnings are mixed, not accelerating: revenue growth has slowed every year since FY23 to 11.37% year-on-year in the latest quarter, the softest of the last eight, because growth now comes almost entirely from price — ARPU up 8.2% in FY26 — while paying-subscriber volume has been flat or negative in three of the last four quarters. The consensus bar is rated fair, but sell-side conviction is fading, with target-price cuts outnumbering raises sixteen to one over three months. The biggest risk is that the current 35.35% EBITDA margin, propped up by deliberately deferred acquisition spend management calls temporary, and the falling subscriber count are the same SME-demand weakness expressed twice, not two offsetting forces. Verdict: mixed earnings setup.

## 1. Earnings Verdict

- **Verdict: Mixed earnings setup**
- Earnings quality /100: **72** *(from 06_earnings-quality — Strong band, but self-capped below 81–100 because ~30% of FY26 Profit Before Tax and ~40% of diluted EPS come from a recurring, non-operating treasury mark-to-market gain that Capital IQ's own structure mislabels "unusual" despite it appearing every year FY22–FY26)*
- Consensus setup /100 *(higher = more beatable)*: **48** *(from 04_guidance-consensus — no partial-data cap applies, consensus and revision history are both present and current; scored in the mixed/average band because the bar is called "fair," not clearly low, revenue/EPS revision breadth is net negative while EBITDA breadth is net positive, and sell-side sentiment is de-rating (target price 1 up / 16 down of 18 analysts; average recommendation drifted Outperform→Hold))*
- Earnings volatility /100 *(higher = WORSE, inverted)*: **66** *(from 07_earnings-sensitivity — High-volatility band; at least three variables can independently swing earnings 20%+ in a single year)*
